paras: The lynching of Pony Poe was the hanging of a Black man by a mob of about 300 men near Bellefontaine, Webster County, Mississippi, in late August 1888. Poe, accused of assaulting three women, was taken from a sheriff's posse on the way to jail and hanged at the scene of the alleged crime. Newspapers across the country carried the story, many noting that he was a former teacher, a leader of the county's Black residents and a recent candidate for public office.

According to a dispatch dated Bellefontaine, Aug. 29, Poe forced his way into the house of a widow, Mrs. Blisset, on a Saturday night and "criminally assaulted" her, her young daughter and a neighbor's 14-year-old daughter after choking them insensible. The same dispatch described Poe as "the leader of the negroes of Webster county," a man who had taught school and had been a candidate for tax assessor the year before. One condensed version called him a former Sunday School teacher.

The next day, a Sunday, the sheriff and a posse arrested Poe at a prayer meeting where he was taking a prominent part in the services. A separate dispatch from Duck Hill placed the capture at a church about twelve miles from the scene of the alleged crime. On Monday, while the posse was taking him to jail, a mob of 300 men overpowered the officers, took Poe to the place of the alleged assault and hanged him.

The Bellefontaine dispatch said Poe confessed, said he deserved death, and admitted assaulting a white woman in north Mississippi years earlier before escaping. It named no witness to this confession, and the Duck Hill dispatch did not mention one.
The coverage names no member of the mob, and no report of an inquest, arrest or official response appears in it.

The story reached readers chiefly through one wire dispatch, which the Grenada Gazette, the only Mississippi paper found, credited to a "Times Democrat Special." Papers from New York to Omaha printed it in full on Aug. 30, while others in Maine, Kentucky and Virginia reduced it to a line or two in their news summaries. Weeklies in Iowa, New Hampshire and Vermont were still reprinting it a week later.

Headlines treated the accusation as fact and the hanging as deserved. The Savannah Morning News ran "The Black Ravish Admits That He Deserved His Fate," the Omaha Daily Bee "A Negro Brute Lynched by Mississippi Vigilantes," and the Leavenworth Advocate "Another Negro Fiend Lynched." The Memphis Appeal called Poe "the negro rapist," and the Grenada Gazette called him "the wretch." A Vermont weekly described the mob as "300 Members of an Outraged Community," while an Iowa paper headed the same text "Mob Law in Mississippi."
The Washington Evening Star used "colored man" in place of "negro" and called Poe "the leader of his race in Webster County."

Both dispatches dated Aug. 29 put the arrest on Sunday and the hanging on Monday. The Western Appeal of St. Paul instead dated the lynching "on the 28th," and a New Hampshire brief put the assault itself on the 29th, apparently reading the dispatch date as the date of the crime. One printing gave the victim's name as "Poney Hoe," and another placed his earlier alleged assault in "North Missouri" rather than north Mississippi.

reader.title: Lynching of Pony Poe
bases: A mob of 300 men took a Black prisoner from a sheriff's posse and hanged him (A2, A10, A21); a separate Duck Hill dispatch says he was taken by 'an armed force' and hanged (A5).

Every report says Poe was hanged after a mob of 300 men overpowered the officers taking him to jail (A2, A4, A10), so he was killed without lawful authority by a large group; the stated reason was his alleged assault on three women (A2, A21).

The widely reprinted Bellefontaine wire dispatch (A2, A4, A10) and a separately worded Duck Hill dispatch in the Memphis Appeal (A5) agree that Poe was captured Sunday and hanged the next day by an armed group, and a Mississippi paper carried a Times-Democrat special to the same effect (A21).

accounts.label: Bellefontaine wire dispatch (Times-Democrat special)
accounts.gist: Poe assaulted three women Saturday night, was arrested at a prayer meeting Sunday, and the next day 300 men took him from the posse and hanged him at the scene after he confessed and said he deserved death.

accounts.label: Duck Hill dispatch
accounts.gist: Poe was captured Sunday at a church about twelve miles from the scene of the crime and on Monday 'taken by an armed force and hanged'; it reports no confession.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'Another Negro Fiend Lynched', 'The Black Ravish Admits That He Deserved His Fate' and 'Negro Strung up by 300 Members of an Outraged Community' presented the lynching as deserved punishment.
The Memphis Appeal called Poe 'the negro rapist' and the Grenada Gazette 'the wretch', treating the accusation as proven.
Most northern papers ran the dispatch as a brief or a one-line item in a news summary, adding only a headline.
The Audubon County Republican headed the dispatch 'Mob Law in Mississippi' while calling the assaults 'brutal'.

versions.value: Monday (Aug. 27), the day after the Sunday arrest

conflicts.note: The Duck Hill and Bellefontaine dispatches, both dated Aug. 29, independently give Sunday arrest and Monday hanging; the later dates look like misreadings of the dispatch date.
'Hoe' appears in one printing of the same wire text and is likely a misprint.
One reprint of the same dispatch; likely a misprint.
The New Hampshire brief's 'posse' compresses the wire text, which distinguishes the sheriff's posse from the mob that overpowered it.

record_check.dossier: Aug. 26 was the Sunday arrest; the hanging was Monday, Aug. 27 (one brief says the 28th).
One victim, Pony (Poney) Poe; 'Poney Hoe' is a misprint of the same name.
Seizure from the sheriff's posse and hanging at the scene of the alleged crime.
A mob of 300 men, none named.
At or near Bellefontaine; the capture was at a church about twelve miles from the scene.

info: Hanged on Monday, the day after his Sunday arrest (Aug. 27, 1888, by the dispatch's datelines); the alleged assault was Saturday night (Aug. 25).
Hanged at the scene of the alleged crime, at or near Bellefontaine, Miss.; captured at a church about twelve miles from that scene.
Pony (also 'Poney') Poe, a Black man; one printing gives 'Poney Hoe'.

Accused of forcing his way into the house of a widow, Mrs. Blisset, on Saturday night and criminally assaulting her, her young daughter and a neighbor's 14-year-old daughter after choking them insensible.
A mob of 300 men; no member was named and their identity is not given.
